analysis.one_liner: Lets states, not the federal government, regulate fracking on federal land inside their borders.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a vote in either chamber and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would give states the only authority to write and enforce rules for hydraulic fracturing — fracking — including on federal land located inside a state, such as national forests and Bureau of Land Management acreage. It would bar federal agencies from imposing their own fracking rules on the land they manage, leaving each state's oil and gas regulations as the only rules that apply. The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal land gain the most: they would face only the rules of the state where they operate, with no possibility of a federal fracking rule imposed by the agency that manages the land. State governments gain sole regulatory control, including over federal land within their borders.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas drillers on federal land

how_it_helps.text: Gives states the sole authority to write and enforce any regulation, guidance, or permit requirement for hydraulic fracturing, eliminating any federal role.

Makes fracking on federal land — national forests, Bureau of Reclamation land, and other federal acreage — subject only to the law of the state where the land sits, so federal land managers could not apply their own fracking rules.

The bill's findings section argues state regulation is already adequate, citing studies and regulators' statements finding no confirmed cases of groundwater contamination from the fracking process itself.

analysis.who_pays: People who live near federal drilling sites and rely on the water and air around them would bear the risk: protections would depend entirely on which state the land is in, with no minimum national standard. All taxpayers, who own federal land in common, would lose a voice in how drilling on that land is conducted.
analysis.who_pays_short: People living near federal drilling sites

drawbacks.text: The bill would leave federal land — which belongs to all Americans — regulated solely under each state's rules, so protections for water and air would vary sharply from state to state and no national minimum would apply.

States that host drilling also collect tax and royalty revenue from it, and the bill sets no baseline requirements, so the level of oversight would rest entirely on each state's own oil and gas regulations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers oil and gas operators a simpler, single-regulator environment and offers states more control, which its sponsors argue is sufficient protection. The cost falls on people near federal drilling sites: federal land is held in trust for everyone, and this bill would let the state containing it — often a state with a direct financial stake in drilling — set whatever fracking rules it chooses, with no federal backstop. Critics of state-only regulation have long pointed to this revenue conflict and the wide variation in state rules as the core weakness, and the bill addresses neither.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator James Inhofe introduced the bill in the Senate on February 7, 2017, joined by eight original cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
Twelve Republican senators total cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The action history shows no further activity — no committee report, hearing, or floor vote — through the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas operators drilling on federal land are no worse off: the status quo they preferred continued, with no federal fracking-specific rule ever taking effect and state regulation remaining the only rulebook.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas operators on federal land

sides.party_line_note: All 12 cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat sponsored or backed the bill; it never reached a vote, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.industry: Oil and gas drillers on federal land
industries.note: The bill would make fracking on federal acreage subject only to state law, eliminating the possibility of a federal fracking rule from the agency that manages the land. Because drilling on that land affects water and air used by neighboring communities and the public at large, the industry's gain here comes at the public's expense.

States would gain sole permitting and rulemaking authority, including over federal land within their borders. Many states do maintain real oil and gas rules, but they also collect revenue from drilling, and the bill sets no minimum national standard.
